lead: An ASIC (application-specific integrated circuit) is a chip made for one product or one job, such as the controller in a smart electricity meter, rather than a standard part like a memory or a microcontroller sold to everyone. ASICs are grouped by how much of the chip is made for that one design. In a full-custom ASIC every transistor is drawn for it. In a standard-cell ASIC the gates come from a pre-designed library, but every mask is still made for it. In a gate-array ASIC the transistors are already built on a stocked base wafer and only the metal wiring is custom. Programmable devices (PLDs and FPGAs) need no custom mask at all. The choice trades design cost and time against the cost, speed, power and size of each chip.
prereq: You need: the stages of the VLSI design flow, especially synthesis, physical design and tapeout.

sections.h3: What makes a chip an ASIC

blocks.text: A standard part is designed once and sold to many customers: a 74-series gate, a DRAM, a general microcontroller. An ASIC is designed for one customer's product. In between sits the ASSP (application-specific standard product): a chip for one kind of job, such as a USB controller, sold to many makers.
ASICs are classified by what is made only for this design. The less that is custom, the lower the one-time cost and the faster the turnaround, but the less efficient the chip.

blocks.text: Some syllabi group standard-cell and gate-array ASICs together as semicustom ASICs. The non-recurring engineering cost (NRE) is the one-time cost of design, tools, masks and test programs; the unit cost is what each further chip costs.

In full-custom design the engineer sizes and draws every transistor in a layout editor, then iterates DRC, LVS and extraction by hand. The result has the best speed, power and area, at the highest design effort. Today it is used for blocks that repeat millions of times or that no tool can build well: SRAM bit cells, standard cells themselves, PLLs, ADCs and high-speed I/O.

In standard-cell design the gates come from a library: inverters, NAND, NOR, AND-OR-invert, multiplexers, flip-flops and adder cells, each in several drive strengths. Every cell in a library has the same height and a width that depends on its function. A VDD rail runs along the top edge and a VSS rail along the bottom, so cells placed side by side in a row join their rails, and alternate rows are flipped to share a rail. The library is characterised: for each cell, files give its delay, power and area at several voltage and temperature corners, so synthesis and timing tools can use it.

Synthesis picks cells, placement puts them in rows and routing joins them in metal above the cells. A standard-cell chip still needs a full mask set, but it can hold hard macros (SRAMs, PLLs) drawn full-custom. Most digital ASICs are built this way.

A masked gate array (MGA) starts from a base wafer that the foundry has already processed up to the transistors. The base is a regular array of base cells, each a few nMOS and pMOS transistors. A design defines only the interconnect: metal on the first layer turns each base cell into a gate (a NAND, an inverter), and higher metal layers wire the gates together. Because the base wafers are stocked, only the few metal and via masks are made for the design.

items: Channelled gate array: rows of base cells with fixed routing channels between the rows.
Channelless gate array (sea of gates): no reserved channels; wires run over unused transistors, so density is higher.
Structured gate array (structured ASIC): the base also holds fixed blocks such as RAM, so memory-heavy designs fit.

blocks.text: Not every transistor of a base can be used: routing blocks some of them, so a design can fill only part of the gates, and the usable fraction depends on the array and the design. Transistor sizes are fixed by the base, so a gate array is slower and less dense than a standard-cell chip of the same function.

sections.h3: Choosing a style: cost against volume

blocks.text: total cost = NRE + N × unit cost,   N<sub>break-even</sub> = (NRE<sub>2</sub> − NRE<sub>1</sub>) ÷ (c<sub>1</sub> − c<sub>2</sub>)
blocks.where: N is the number of chips and c the cost of each chip. Option 2 has the larger NRE and the smaller c; above the break-even volume it is cheaper in total.

blocks.text: Cost is not the only test. A standard-cell chip takes months from netlist to silicon and a bug after tapeout needs new masks (a respin), while an FPGA bug is fixed by loading a new configuration. So a product with an early deadline or an unfinished standard may start on an FPGA and move to an ASIC once the volume is known.

figure.caption: Three ASIC styles with the worked example’s costs. Full-custom draws every shape; a standard-cell chip places library cells of one height in rows between VDD and VSS rails; a gate array starts from a stocked base of identical cells and adds only the metal wiring, so its NRE is lowest of the three and its cost per chip highest.

spec.aria: Three panels: hand-drawn full-custom shapes, rows of equal-height standard cells between supply rails, and a grid of identical gate-array base cells joined by metal wires, each with its NRE and cost per chip.

examples.question: A smart-meter controller can be built four ways. FPGA: NRE ₹0, ₹1,800 per chip. Gate array: NRE ₹40 lakh, ₹500 per chip. Standard cell: NRE ₹2 crore, ₹250 per chip. Full custom: NRE ₹8 crore, ₹200 per chip. (a) Find the total cost of each for 50,000 meters. (b) Find the break-even volumes between neighbouring options. (c) Which is cheapest for 2,000, 50,000 and 20 lakh meters?
steps: Gate array: ₹40 lakh + 50,000 × ₹500 = ₹40 lakh + ₹250 lakh = ₹2.90 crore.
Standard cell: ₹200 lakh + 50,000 × ₹250 = ₹200 lakh + ₹125 lakh = ₹3.25 crore.
Full custom: ₹800 lakh + 50,000 × ₹200 = ₹800 lakh + ₹100 lakh = ₹9.00 crore.
Standard cell to full custom: (₹8 crore − ₹2 crore) ÷ (250 − 200) = ₹6,00,00,000 ÷ 50 = 12 lakh chips.
(c) 2,000 is below 3,077, so the FPGA is cheapest: ₹36 lakh against ₹50 lakh for the gate array.
50,000 lies between 3,077 and 64,000, so the gate array is cheapest (₹2.90 crore), as part (a) showed.
20 lakh is above 12 lakh: full custom costs ₹8 crore + ₹40 crore = ₹48 crore against ₹2 crore + ₹50 crore = ₹52 crore for standard cell.
examples.answer: (a) ₹9.00 crore, ₹2.90 crore, ₹3.25 crore and ₹9.00 crore. (b) 3,077, 64,000 and 12 lakh chips. (c) FPGA for 2,000, gate array for 50,000 and full custom for 20 lakh, if the full-custom schedule (often a year or more longer) is acceptable; otherwise standard cell.

traps: An ASIC is not the same as full-custom. Most ASICs are standard-cell designs; full-custom is one style among several.
A masked gate array is not an FPGA. The gate array is wired by metal masks at the foundry and cannot change afterwards; the FPGA is configured by the user.
Standard cells share one height, not one width. The width changes with the function and the drive strength.
Break-even volume is the difference in NRE divided by the difference in unit cost. NRE divided by a single unit cost means nothing.
The lowest total cost is not the whole answer. Time to market and the cost of a respin can rule out the cheapest style.

quiz.q: Name the classes of ASIC by how much of the chip is customised.
quiz.a: Full-custom; semicustom, which is standard-cell (cell-based) or masked gate array; and programmable (PLDs and FPGAs).

quiz.q: Which masks are made for one design in a masked gate array?
quiz.a: Only the interconnect masks: contacts, vias and metal layers. The transistor layers are already on the stocked base wafer.

quiz.q: Why do all cells of a standard-cell library have the same height?
quiz.a: So that any cell fits any site in a row and the VDD and VSS rails of neighbouring cells join into continuous rails. Only the width changes from cell to cell.

quiz.q: How does a sea-of-gates array differ from a channelled gate array?
quiz.a: A channelled array reserves routing channels between rows of base cells. A sea of gates has no reserved channels; wires run over unused transistors, which raises density.

quiz.q: A gate array has NRE ₹60 lakh and costs ₹300 per chip; an FPGA costs ₹1,500 per chip. Find the break-even volume.
A sea-of-gates base has 2,00,000 gates and 70 % of them can be used. Does a 1,50,000-gate design fit?
quiz.a: Usable gates = 0.70 × 2,00,000 = 1,40,000, which is less than 1,50,000, so it does not fit. It needs a base of at least 1,50,000 ÷ 0.70 = 2,14,286 gates.

quiz.q: At 30,000 chips a gate array is cheaper than a standard-cell ASIC. Give two reasons a team may still choose standard cell.
quiz.a: Standard cells give higher speed, lower power and smaller die area, which a battery or high-clock product may need. A volume forecast above the break-even (64,000 in the worked example) or memory and analog blocks that a fixed base cannot hold also favour standard cell.

quiz.q: Why does a gate array reach silicon in weeks while a standard-cell chip takes months?
quiz.a: The gate-array base wafers are already processed up to the transistors and kept in stock, so only a few metal layers are made and processed. A standard-cell chip needs every mask and the full wafer process from bare silicon.

beyond: Not for the exam. Multi-project wafers share one mask set among many small designs, which brings a student or start-up chip down to a small slice of the NRE. Open process design kits such as SkyWater SKY130 with the OpenROAD flow let anyone build a standard-cell chip from free tools. Structured ASICs and FPGA-to-ASIC conversion services sit between gate arrays and FPGAs. Search next: multi-project wafer, structured ASIC, SKY130 open PDK and the Liberty format for cell libraries.
